proposed_edges.relationship: Métis peoplehood, not 'mixedness': the 'simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity' in scholarship on Métis histories misrecognize the Métis as 'a hybrid off-shoot of two races' rather than an Indigenous people (2014)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words, 'Métis': Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (UBC Press, 2014), introduction read in the publisher's sample (pp. 3–14): p. 4, 'an overly racialized narrative that connected Métis nationhood to fur trade society'; p. 5, 'the simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity that seem to fascinate so many scholars who write of Métis histories'; p. 6, 'misrecognized as a hybrid off-shoot of two races … rather than as an Indigenous people'; p. 10, 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?'; p. 11, 'To continue to understand the Métis in terms of some apparently innate mixedness is thus to reproduce the same racist depictions'; p. 12, chapter 1 treats 'a strand of long-standing fur trade literature'. In the pages read he names no fur-trade historian, so the arrow targets the frame, not Van Kirk, Brown or Peterson. Their side in their own words: Peers and Podruchny (2010, n. 2) use 'metis' for 'all descendants of European men and Aboriginal women'; Brown, as translated there (pp. 2–3, n. 3): 'there is no single Metis core identity but rather a range along a spectrum'; Brown (2017, p. 57 n. 26) names The New Peoples and Andersen's book as the older and newer poles of the field and (pp. 57–58) offers 'of mixed descent' as a descriptive term beside 'the natives’ own categories'. Chapters 1–5 unread. Person entry, identity note and the book's source record are Agent B's. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §§2.1–2.2)

proposed_edges.relationship: Judges James Walker's survey of Canadian historical writing about Indigenous peoples 'eye-opening' but 'conservative and inadequate': 'Canadian historiography is not that benign' (1999)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, dissertation (University of Manitoba, 1999), PDF p. 119, read by Agent B (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md §1.7): 'I find James Walker's assessment of Canadian historical writing conservative and inadequate. While Walker's article is an eye-opening and ground-breaking re-assessment of Canadian historiography … it does not go deep enough'; against his conclusion that the times made prejudice inevitable: 'Does any time ever make prejudice … “inevitable”? Canadian historiography is not that benign'. Walker's 1971 survey (nnreq_walker_1971) is in this strand; he has no node. edge_868 (indigenous → native_newcomer) already carries LaRocque at field level; this is the person-level, strand-level arrow. Requested by Agent B (ihB_rel_16).

proposed_edges.relationship: Reads Trigger's foreword to Sioui's Autohistory, which praised it for never descending 'to recrimination', as 'a typical example of containment' of Native resistance writing (1999)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, dissertation (1999), PDF pp. 135–136, read by Agent B (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md §1.7): Native works are 'gauged with a language of containment. Bruce Trigger's foreword to George Sioui's For An American [sic] Autohistory provides a typical example of containment'; scholars 'must make it their mandate first to comprehend the noxious nature of colonization before dismissing utterances of decolonization merely as “sloganistic,” “bitter,” “biased” or “polemical”' (p. 136). Trigger has no node; the arrow goes to the strand that holds his contact-era work. Sioui is not the target. Requested by Agent B (ihB_rel_17).

row.context: Criticises fur-trade, judicial and census readings of Métis as 'mixed' and places Métis peoplehood in a Red River historical core (2014). A critic of the frame, not a member; no identity classification is recorded on this roster.
row.works: 'Métis': Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (2014)

row.context: With Podruchny, the field's 2010 account of itself: Aboriginal history as 'one of the most significant changes in Canadian historiography since the 1970s', and a critique of archive-only work.
Co-author of the Saskatchewan treaty history, drawn 'on a wide range of documentary sources' (publisher's description).
row.works: Bounty and Benevolence (2000, with Ray and Miller)

row.context: Disease, starvation policy and the loss of Aboriginal life on the plains (2013). Roster row only, under the settler-scholar citation rule.

new_sources.title: Laura Peers and Carolyn Podruchny, 'Introduction: Complex Subjectivities, Multiple Ways of Knowing', in Peers and Podruchny, eds., Gathering Places: Aboriginal and Fur Trade Histories (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2010), 1–17.
new_sources.citation: Laura Peers and Carolyn Podruchny, 'Introduction: Complex Subjectivities, Multiple Ways of Knowing', in Peers and Podruchny, eds., Gathering Places: Aboriginal and Fur Trade Histories (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2010), 1–17.

verification.note: Introduction and notes 1–31 read in full in the publisher's sample PDF (UBC Press asset 9448). p. 1: 'One of the most significant changes in Canadian historiography since the 1970s has been the development of Aboriginal history as a vibrant and challenging part of the discipline'; 'Recent Aboriginal history has moved far beyond older narratives in which actions by the Indian and the European were understood from scholarly perspectives that generally lacked an understanding of Aboriginal cultures'; pp. 2–3 quote Brown, 'Noms et métaphores' (their translation, n. 3): 'there is no single Metis core identity but rather a range along a spectrum'; n. 2: 'metis' for 'all descendants of European men and Aboriginal women', 'Metis' for the historic Metis Nation; p. 3: 'The most advanced work on Aboriginal history in Canada … has grown out of trends in ethnohistory and cultural history'; pp. 11–12: 'academic blindness to, Aboriginal signatures and artifacts' bound by 'shallow ethnocentric interpretations'; p. 12: taking seriously what community members say 'has been discussed far more in anthropology than in Canadian history'; 'Most historians are still non-Aboriginal'. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §3.1)
